agents.name: Goose
agents.mcp: first-class — every tool is an MCP server
agents.interesting: Pure MCP-first architecture: the agent itself is a thin shell, every capability (memory, search, files) is a swappable MCP server. Treats memory as a tool you bring, not a feature it ships.

agents.name: Claude Code (Anthropic)
agents.interesting: Memory-as-files. Every memory is a markdown file you can grep, version, diff, edit. No vector DB. The 'index' is your filesystem. Auditable by design.

agents.name: Hermes Agent
agents.interesting: Algebraic memory instead of semantic chunks. HRR lets you compose/decompose memories with vector arithmetic. Novel; the storage is boring SQLite, the cleverness is the representation.

agents.name: Honcho
agents.interesting: Middleware — sits in front of any LLM app and adds peer-centric memory. Async reasoning derives 'conclusions' about each user. Not a full agent, a memory layer.

agents.name: Letta (was MemGPT)
agents.interesting: Tiered memory: core (in context) + recall (recent history) + archival (vector search). The reference implementation for 'agent with batteries-included memory.' Worth reading even if you don't use it.

agents.name: Mem0
agents.interesting: Multi-level: User / Session / Agent. Single-pass extraction + entity linking. Memory-as-a-service shape — opinionated about hierarchy, less about backend.

agents.name: Zep
agents.interesting: Time-aware memory. Every fact has a 'valid_at' window. The bet: temporal context matters as much as semantic similarity. Niche but right for some use cases.

agents.name: Cognee
agents.interesting: Knowledge-graph-first. Embeddings are secondary, relationships primary. Heavy if your data isn't relational; powerful if it is.

agents.name: LangGraph
agents.interesting: Splits memory into 'checkpoint' (run state) and 'Store' (long-term). Not a memory system itself, but the split has been adopted by other frameworks.

agents.name: Dust
agents.interesting: Production at scale. Their published case studies show vector DB tuning becomes the bottleneck before retrieval quality does. Reference for 'this works in a real org.'

patterns.title: There's no consensus storage backend
patterns.detail: Postgres for stateful servers (Letta, Honcho, LangGraph). Filesystem for sandboxed agents (Claude). SQLite for local dev. Pick by deployment, not by trend.

patterns.title: Almost no one ships their own embeddings
patterns.detail: Every framework defers to OpenAI / Anthropic / Ollama. text-embedding-3-small is the default-of-defaults. This means: pick your embedding model independently of your framework.

patterns.title: The memory-tier split is real and worth copying
patterns.detail: Letta's core/recall/archival and LangGraph's checkpoint/Store both reflect the same insight: short-term context and long-term retrieval are different problems. Don't try to solve them in one layer.

patterns.title: MCP adoption is bimodal
patterns.detail: Goose and Claude treat MCP as first-class. Most others don't mention it. If you're in the Anthropic ecosystem, lean into MCP. Otherwise it's optional.

patterns.title: Filesystem-based memory is having a moment
patterns.detail: Anthropic's bet: files are the simplest, most auditable, most portable memory. They version, diff, grep. No DB to migrate. No schema to evolve. For personal/team scale, it's hard to beat.
